subject: arvr
title: Unit 2 MCQs — Graphical System, Programming and 3D Modelling

items.q: In computer graphics, **modelling** and **rendering** refer respectively to:
options: Generating images, and storing them on disk
Creating/manipulating/storing geometric objects, and generating their images
Defining the camera, and defining the lights
items.explain: **Modelling** = creation, manipulation and storage of geometric objects — defining shape and structure. **Rendering** = transforming those models into visually perceivable images via lighting, shading, texturing and rasterization.

items.q: In the pen plotter model, which pair of functions forms the entire API?
items.explain: **`moveto(x,y)`** repositions the pen **without drawing**; **`lineto(x,y)`** draws from the current position to the new one. Note the model is **stateful** — `lineto` draws from *'the current position'*, an idea that survives into OpenGL's state machine.

items.q: Which is a stated **limitation** of the pen plotter model?
options: It does not extend well to 3D graphics and lacks real-time rendering
items.explain: It operates **strictly in 2D**, **lacks real-time rendering**, and is slower and less adaptable than raster displays for complex effects. It is however excellent at precise vector output — hence its survival in CNC plotting and drafting.

items.q: The key function of the raster-based 2D model is:
items.explain: **`write_pixel(x, y, color)`** sets one pixel in the **framebuffer**. This gives fine-grained control (shading, anti-aliasing, texturing) but loses structural information about objects and is memory-intensive.

items.q: Which four components must a three-dimensional API let you specify?
options: Objects, viewer, light sources, material properties
items.explain: **Objects** (sets of vertices), **viewer** (camera position & orientation), **light sources** (directional, spot, point) and **material properties** (absorption, scattering, diffuse/specular). These are the four things needed to answer *'what colour is this pixel?'*

items.q: What is a **display list**?
options: Image instructions stored in memory and executed repeatedly to maintain the display without flicker
The ordered list of objects sorted by depth
A queue of pending user input events
items.explain: It frees the CPU from re-describing the picture every refresh — the display processor replays it. The same idea survives as the modern **vertex buffer object (VBO)**: upload once, draw with one call per frame.

items.q: What is the correct order of the four major steps in the imaging process?
options: Rasterization → Vertex processing → Clipping → Fragment processing
Vertex processing → Clipping and primitive assembly → Rasterization → Fragment processing
Clipping → Rasterization → Vertex processing → Fragment processing
Vertex processing → Rasterization → Clipping → Fragment processing
items.explain: **① Vertex processing** (transform + light per vertex) → **② Clipping and primitive assembly** (cull what's outside the view volume) → **③ Rasterization** (primitives become fragments) → **④ Fragment processing** (texture, depth test, final colour).

items.q: In the graphics pipeline, a **fragment** is:
options: A finished pixel written to the framebuffer
A candidate pixel carrying colour, depth and texture data, which may still be discarded
A vertex that failed the clipping test
items.explain: A fragment is a **candidate**. It may be discarded by the depth or alpha test, or blended with others — several fragments can compete for one pixel. Fragment ≠ pixel.

items.q: Early graphics systems used calligraphic CRT displays, which required:
options: High refresh rates to avoid flicker
items.explain: A calligraphic (vector) CRT steers the beam **along the lines of the drawing**; the image fades unless retraced, so **high refresh rates were needed to avoid flicker**. The display list was the fix.

items.q: Which two pipeline stages are programmable?
items.explain: **Vertex shaders** replace stage ① and **fragment shaders** replace stage ④. Clipping and rasterization remain **fixed-function** — they are pure geometry with no artistic decisions to make.

items.q: A vertex program (vertex shader) is responsible for:
options: Applying textures and transparency to pixels
Modifying vertex positions, computing vertex colours, and performing custom transformations
Determining which pixels lie inside a triangle
Removing primitives outside the clipping volume
items.explain: Vertex shaders handle **morphing/deformation/animation**, **lighting-based vertex colours**, and **custom transformations beyond traditional matrix operations**. Texturing and transparency are the **fragment** shader's job.

items.q: Roughly how many times does a fragment shader run compared with a vertex shader, for one full-screen triangle at 1080p?
options: Hundreds of thousands of times more
items.explain: 3 vertices versus roughly **two million fragments**. This is why work that can be done per-vertex and interpolated is thousands of times cheaper — the single most important optimisation principle in real-time graphics.

items.q: A 2D point $p = (x,y)$ corresponds to which point in 3D?
items.explain: $(x, y, 0)$ — which is why there is no separate 2D graphics system. In homogeneous form it is $(x, y, 0, 1)$: $z=0$ because it lies on the plane, $w=1$ because it is a **point**.

items.q: Normalized Device Coordinates in OpenGL typically span which range?
items.explain: **$[-1,1]$** — a canonical cube. Being resolution-independent means the same scene renders identically at any resolution, clipping is done against a fixed volume, and a headset can render two viewports from one NDC scene.

items.q: In the Sierpinski gasket's random algorithm, each new point is:
options: A random point inside the triangle
The midpoint between the current point and a randomly selected vertex
The centroid of the three vertices
A reflection of the current point about the nearest edge
items.explain: Pick one of the three vertices **at random**, take the **midpoint** between it and the current point, plot it, and repeat. Despite the randomness the structure converges to a **highly ordered, self-similar fractal**.

items.q: Why is the 'use GPU for display' version of the gasket faster than drawing each point immediately?
options: The GPU generates the points itself
The point data is uploaded once and replayed from GPU memory, instead of the CPU issuing a call per point
items.explain: Immediate mode means the CPU talks to the graphics system **once per point** (100,000 times). Uploading once and drawing from GPU memory replaces that with a **single draw call** — the display-list idea, as a VBO.

items.q: Which is **NOT** one of the six categories of API functions?
items.explain: The six are **Primitive, Attribute, Viewing, Transformation, Input and Control**. They answer: what shapes · what do they look like · from where · positioned how · how does the user act · how is the program managed.

items.q: What does **GLEW** provide?
options: Management of OpenGL extensions, eliminating platform-specific dependencies
items.explain: **GLEW** = OpenGL **Extension Wrangler** — it manages extensions so you can use modern features without manual extension loading. **GLUT** does windowing and input; **GL** is the core rendering library.

items.q: What is the difference between `glColor3d` and `glColor3f`?
options: `glColor3d` allows 3D colour operations while `glColor3f` allows only 8-bit
`glColor3d` takes double arguments while `glColor3f` takes float arguments
`glColor3d` is in real space while `glColor3f` is in integer space
items.explain: The suffix is always **count then type**: `3` = three components, `d` = double, `f` = float. Both set R, G and B. Reading `3d` as '3-dimensional' is the trap.

items.q: In `glVertex3fv`, what does the trailing `v` mean?
options: The arguments are passed as a vector (an array)
The values are in view coordinates
items.explain: **`v` = vector form** — the components are passed as an array rather than as separate arguments. Hence `glVertex2dv(array[i])` in the gasket code.

items.q: Which is a property of **raster** primitives?
options: They have definable points and edges in 3D space
They exist as arrays of pixels in the framebuffer and undergo no geometric transformation
They are transformed, clipped, lit and shaded
They scale without loss of quality
items.explain: Raster primitives **lack geometric structure**, live as pixels in the framebuffer, and follow a **separate rasterization pipeline** concerned with blending, filtering and anti-aliasing — not transformation.

items.q: Which is the correct list of primitive types available to `glBegin`?
options: GL_QUADS, GL_TRIANGLES, GL_LINES, GL_LINE_STRIP, GL_QUAD_STRIP, GL_LINE_LOOP, GL_TRIANGLE_STRIP, GL_POINTS, GL_POLYGON
items.explain: The names are **plural** — `GL_POINTS`, `GL_LINES`, `GL_TRIANGLES`, `GL_QUADS`. The singular list is the deliberate distractor.

items.q: Given vertices $v_0 \dots v_5$, how many triangles does `GL_TRIANGLE_STRIP` produce?
items.explain: A strip gives $n - 2$ triangles, so $6 - 2 = \mathbf{4}$. `GL_TRIANGLES` would give only 2 from the same 6 vertices — strips exist precisely to avoid re-sending shared vertices.

items.q: What primitive polygon is generally used for creating a mesh to represent a complex object?
items.explain: The **triangle** — it is always **planar** (3 points define a plane), always **convex**, trivial to rasterize, and supports barycentric interpolation naturally. Quads may be non-planar, leaving the surface ill-defined.

items.q: Which rendering method is described as the **most common in real-time rendering and game graphics**?
options: Render the interior with solid colour or patterns
Choose to render or not render edges (cel-shading)
items.explain: Filling faces with a colour, gradient or texture. **Wireframe** is for debugging and modelling; **selective edges** is for stylised looks like cel-shading.

items.q: A **simple polygon** is one in which:
options: There are at most four vertices
All interior angles are less than 180°
items.explain: No self-intersection, so the interior is unambiguous. OpenGL assumes polygons are **simple, convex and planar** and does **not check** — feeding it a complex polygon gives undefined behaviour.

items.q: `glutInitWindowSize()` sets the window size. What happens if it is not called?
options: OpenGL uses the previously set value
items.explain: GLUT defaults to **300 × 300**.

items.q: What happens to code placed **after** `glutMainLoop()`?
options: It runs after the window closes
It never runs — `glutMainLoop()` does not return
It runs once before the first frame
items.explain: `glutMainLoop()` **never returns** — control passes permanently to GLUT, which invokes your registered callbacks on events. This inversion of control is what 'event-driven' means.

items.q: What is the purpose of `glPushMatrix()` and `glPopMatrix()`?
options: To switch between projection and model-view matrices
To save and restore the current matrix, giving scoped transformations
To upload a matrix to the GPU
items.explain: `glPushMatrix` saves a copy of the current matrix on a stack; `glPopMatrix` restores it. Changes between them affect only what is drawn inside — preventing transforms from **leaking** into subsequent objects and frames.

items.q: To first **rotate** an object and then **move** it to a new position, in what order should the OpenGL calls be issued?
options: Either order — the result is the same
items.explain: With column vectors the **last matrix issued is applied first**. Issuing `glTranslatef` then `glRotatef` builds $T \cdot R$, so the rotation acts on the object first and the translation afterwards.

items.q: What do the nine arguments of `gluLookAt` specify?
options: Three vertices of the near plane
Eye position, look-at point, and up vector
Field of view, aspect ratio and clipping planes
items.explain: **Eye** (where the camera is), **centre** (what it looks at) and **up** (which way is up). Eye fixes position, centre fixes direction, and up pins the remaining **roll** freedom — six degrees of freedom in total.

items.q: If you need more **shininess** on an object, which light/material property would you change?
items.explain: **Specular** scattering produces the mirror-like highlight and depends on the **viewing direction** — which is why the highlight slides across a surface as you move, and why it reads as *shiny*. Diffuse is view-independent and matte.

items.q: In the modelling–rendering paradigm, what does the **interface file** contain?
options: Object descriptions, light sources and viewer location
items.explain: The interface file is the seam between modeller and renderer, carrying everything needed to produce the image. Today this is a **glTF file** between **Blender** and **Three.js** — the same architecture, forty years on.

items.q: In an **orthographic** projection, the projectors are:
options: Convergent at the centre of projection
items.explain: **Perpendicular** to the view plane, so objects appear without distortion and **actual dimensions are preserved** — hence its use in blueprints and CAD. If the projectors meet the plane at any other angle it is **oblique**.

items.q: Which oblique projection **scales depth down** to create a more natural look?
items.explain: **Cabinet** halves the depth; **cavalier** preserves it fully and looks stretched, because the eye expects depth to foreshorten. Cabinet is a deliberate compromise between measurability and realism.

items.q: In perspective projection, the projectors converge at:
items.explain: The **centre of projection**, mimicking the eye. **Vanishing points** are where *parallel lines in the scene* appear to converge in the image — a different thing.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes parallel from perspective projection?
options: Parallel projection distorts dimensions; perspective preserves them
In parallel projection the distance from the centre of projection is infinite; in perspective it is finite
Parallel projection has three types; perspective has two
Parallel projection creates realistic views; perspective does not
items.explain: This is the row that explains all the others — **parallel projection is perspective projection with the eye moved infinitely far away**, so projectors become parallel and foreshortening vanishes. Parallel has **two** types (orthographic, oblique); perspective has **three** (one-, two-, three-point).

items.q: A drawing of a skyscraper viewed from street level, with vertical edges converging upward, uses:
items.explain: **Three-point** — the third vanishing point sits above (or below) the horizon, making the **vertical** edges converge and creating a sense of height. Count vanishing points by counting how many sets of parallel edges recede.

items.q: What is the key difference between `glOrtho()` and `gluPerspective()`?
options: `glOrtho` defines a rectangular box view volume; `gluPerspective` defines a frustum
`glOrtho` is for 2D only; `gluPerspective` is for 3D only
items.explain: `glOrtho(l,r,b,t,n,f)` gives a **box** with parallel projectors and no depth effect; `gluPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far)` gives a **frustum** with converging projectors, so distant objects shrink. ⚠ Never call both without `glLoadIdentity()` between them — they multiply into the same matrix.

items.q: Which three objects are mandatory for anything to render in Three.js?
items.explain: **Scene** (the graph root), **Camera** (the viewer) and **Renderer** (draws scene from camera into a canvas). A visible object additionally needs a **Mesh = Geometry + Material**.

items.q: `new THREE.PerspectiveCamera(75, aspect, 0.1, 1000)` — these four arguments correspond to which classical OpenGL call?
items.explain: **`gluPerspective(fovy, aspect, near, far)`** — identical arguments in the same order. Three.js is a layer over WebGL, which is OpenGL ES; the concepts are unchanged.

items.q: A Three.js scene renders as a black screen. Which is **NOT** a likely cause?
options: No light in the scene while using MeshStandardMaterial
The camera is at the origin, inside the object
The render loop was never started
The geometry has too many segments
items.explain: Too many segments costs **performance**, not visibility. The three classic causes are **no light** (with a lit material), **camera inside the object** (both default to the origin), and **no render loop**.

items.q: Which Three.js material **ignores lights entirely**?
items.explain: **MeshBasicMaterial** is unlit — useful for UI, wireframes and debugging (it always shows, even with no lights). Lambert adds **diffuse**, Phong adds **specular**, Standard is **physically based** (roughness/metalness).

items.q: Which texture maps should be tagged as **sRGB** colour space?
options: Only colour maps such as `map` and `emissiveMap`
Only data maps such as `normalMap` and `roughnessMap`
items.explain: **Only colour maps.** Data maps (normal, roughness, metalness, AO) store *numbers*, not colours, and must stay **linear**. Tagging a normal map as sRGB silently corrupts the lighting.

items.q: Why must `geometry.dispose()` and `material.dispose()` be called?
options: To remove the object from the scene graph
Because JavaScript's garbage collector cannot free GPU memory
items.explain: Removing a mesh frees the JS object but leaves its **buffers and textures resident on the GPU**. In a long AR/VR session that loads and unloads content this is a genuine leak. (React Three Fiber does this automatically on unmount.)

items.q: Why is `cube.rotation.y += 0.01` inside the render loop considered a bug?
options: Rotation must be set with a quaternion
The rotation speed depends on the frame rate, so it differs across machines
items.explain: At 60 fps this is 0.6 rad/s; at 144 fps it is 1.44 rad/s. Scale by **delta time** — `+= 1.0 * delta` — to get one radian per **second** regardless of hardware. Critical in VR, where headsets run at 72/90/120 Hz.

items.q: In a Three.js + physics-engine application, what is the correct per-frame order?
options: Step physics → copy transforms to meshes → render
Physics and rendering run independently with no copying
items.explain: **Step, copy, render.** The physics world owns position and orientation; Three.js owns appearance; you synchronise them by copying each frame. Almost every physics bug in such an app is a synchronisation mistake.

items.q: Why should a physics engine be stepped at a **fixed** timestep rather than with the raw frame delta?
options: Fixed steps are faster to compute
Simulations are only stable at a fixed step; variable deltas make behaviour hardware-dependent and can explode
items.explain: Physics integrators are tuned for a constant step (typically 1/60 s). The standard fix is an **accumulator** that runs zero or more fixed steps per frame — decoupling physics rate from render rate, which matters in VR where the headset dictates the frame rate.

items.q: In the modelling–rendering paradigm applied to modern web AR, which component plays the role of the **interface file**?
items.explain: **Blender** is the modeller, **glTF/.glb** is the interface file, **Three.js** is the renderer. glTF carries meshes, materials, textures, skeletons and animations — often called 'the JPEG of 3D'.

items.q: Blender is Z-up while glTF and Three.js are Y-up. What is the consequence if this is mishandled?
options: Models arrive rotated — typically lying on their back
items.explain: The glTF exporter converts automatically, but hand-moved data or odd transform handling produces models **lying on their back**. Rotating by −90° about X in Three.js to compensate is a symptom, not a cure — fix it at export.

items.q: What does **UV unwrapping** do?
options: Flattens the 3D surface into a 2D layout so textures can be mapped onto it
items.explain: It defines the mapping between the 3D surface and the 2D texture image — you mark **seams**, unwrap, and arrange the **UV islands**. **A model with no UVs cannot be textured**, and will render as flat colour whatever maps you assign.

items.q: In React Three Fiber, what does the `args` prop do?
options: Sets properties on the instance after creation
Passes arguments to the underlying Three.js **constructor**
items.explain: `args={[1,1,1]}` on `<boxGeometry>` means `new THREE.BoxGeometry(1,1,1)`. Ordinary props (`position`, `color`) are **set on the instance**. That is the whole convention.

items.q: Why should you never call `setState` inside `useFrame`?
options: `useFrame` does not have access to state
It triggers a React re-render up to 120 times a second, destroying performance
State updates are ignored during animation
It would break the scene graph
items.explain: Mutate through a **ref** instead (`ref.current.rotation.y += delta`). React state is for things that change **occasionally** (hovered, selected); refs are for things that change **every frame**.

items.q: Which statement about React Three Fiber is correct?
options: It is a re-implementation of Three.js in React
It is a React renderer that builds real Three.js objects from a declarative component tree
It replaces WebGL with the DOM
It only supports a fixed set of predefined components
items.explain: R3F is **not a wrapper or a rewrite** — it constructs genuine Three.js objects. The **entire Three.js namespace** is available as lower-case JSX elements automatically, so everything you know still applies.

items.q: When entering an immersive WebXR session, `requestAnimationFrame` must be replaced by:
items.explain: The **headset** drives frame timing (72/90/120 Hz), independently of the browser's display refresh. Keeping `requestAnimationFrame` means the loop stops or runs at the wrong rate — the most common WebXR porting mistake.

items.q: Which WebXR **reference space** should a standing, room-scale experience use so that $y = 0$ is the real floor?
items.explain: **`local-floor`** puts the origin at floor level, so real-world scale is correct. With `local` the system does not know where the floor is, and avatars float or sink — the usual cause of 'everything is the wrong height'.

items.q: What does WebXR **hit testing** provide?
options: Where a ray from the device intersects the device's model of the real world
Whether the user's controller button was pressed
The frame rate of the headset
items.explain: It reports where a ray lands on a detected real surface — floor, table, wall — and is the mechanism behind every 'tap to place' AR app. It depends on the device's **SLAM-based world model**, which Unit 4 explains.

items.q: Why does an `immersive-ar` session require a transparent clear colour?
options: So the real world remains visible behind the virtual content
Because AR devices cannot render backgrounds
items.explain: In AR the real world shows through, so an opaque background or skybox would hide it. This is Unit 3's **AR vs VR** distinction expressed as a rendering setting.
